clue.text: US retreating, pawn and bishop hemming queen, excellent!

indicators.note: A hem runs along the edges of a cloth, so the letters on either side of the word close round what sits between them.
Anything retreating goes back the way it came, so the letters named before it are written in the opposite order.

parts.note: the two letters of the country written back to front
p = pawn, as the piece is written on a chess scoresheet
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher that was stamped on British postboxes
b = bishop, the other chessman shortened to its initial

explanation.surface: The Americans falling back while two chessmen close in on the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The queen here is the British one rather than the chessboard's, and the pawn and bishop stay on the board around her. The exclamation mark belongs to the definition, which is a shout of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Superb is praise at full strength, said of a thing so good it needs nothing qualifying it, which is what excellent claims.

indicators.note: Something done recklessly is done without care for how it comes out, so the letters beside it will not stay in the order they were handed over in.
To dodge a thing is to get out of its way, so the letter named next is never there to be used.

parts.note: the six letters of the word with the R dropped, the five left over re-set
R is resistance in physics, the letter Ohm's law uses, and it is the one dodged

explanation.surface: Chasing after something hard enough to slip past whatever stands in the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash does a link word's job, cutting the definition off from the instruction that follows. Two things happen to one word here: a letter leaves and what remains is re-ordered.
explanation.definitionFit: To use up a supply is to take the last of it and leave none, which is to finish it off.

clue.text: Feature French city near the beginning

parts.note: an ear is a feature of the head
Lyon stands where the Saône meets the Rhône and is France's third city

explanation.surface: A magazine planning to run a French city near the front of the issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feature' wants to be the verb an editor uses and it is the noun on the side of your head. The join falls inside the second word of the answer, not between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens early on happens near the beginning of whatever stretch of time is being described.

clue.text: Aha! Each character taking one step on apron

indicators.note: A character is a letter here, and a letter that takes one step moves one place further along the alphabet.

parts.note: A, H and A each advanced by one place in the alphabet

explanation.surface: A cry of discovery as everybody takes a step out onto the apron.
explanation.walkthrough: Shifting every letter one place along the alphabet is a rare device, worth storing for the next time a short exclamation turns up. The apron is the cloth tied under a child's chin, not the tarmac beside a terminal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bib is the cloth tied on to keep a child's front clean at mealtimes, an apron that covers only the chest.

clue.text: Well-known photo containing Bublé without clothing

indicators.note: What contains a thing holds it inside, so the letters named before close round the ones that follow.
Clothing is what goes on the outside, so a name without it gives up the letter at each of its ends.

parts.note: a pic is a photo, and it opens to take something in
Michael Bublé, the Canadian singer of standards, stripped of the letter at each end

explanation.surface: A famous photograph with an undressed Michael Bublé somewhere inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: The accent on the singer's last letter does not save it from being stripped off with the rest of his clothing. 'Well-known' reads as a description of the photo and is doing the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: A public figure is one whose name has travelled beyond the people who actually know them, which is what being well-known amounts to.

clue.text: Time taken to get issue ready for delivery?

definitions.text: Time taken to get issue ready for delivery?

parts.words: Time taken to get issue ready
parts.note: the surface offers a print shop's schedule: the hours it takes to put an issue of a magazine to bed
delivery sounds like the van at the door, but the setter means birth, and the issue is offspring rather than a print run

explanation.surface: A magazine working out how long it needs before the issue can go out.
explanation.walkthrough: Issue is the word doing double duty: a number of a periodical, and the old legal word for a person's children. Nine months is the human answer, and the question mark is the only warning that the sentence has a second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Pregnancy is the whole term a child is carried for, ending in delivery, so the clue reads straight once issue means offspring.

indicators.note: A thing inside another is enclosed by it, so the letters named first go within the ones named next.

parts.note: B&M is a British discount chain, and its name is the two letters with nothing but an ampersand between them
the loo is the British household word for the toilet

explanation.surface: A flush toilet on sale in the aisles of a discount store.
explanation.walkthrough: The shop's ampersand is punctuation, so the letters on either side of it simply stand apart. 'Flush' looks like part of the plumbing and is the noun for a sudden burst of colour or growth.
explanation.definitionFit: A flush of growth or colour is a bloom — the same sudden flowering, whether on a rose bush or in somebody's cheeks.

clue.text: Passionate contribution to explain ten secrets

indicators.note: A contribution to something is a part of it, so a run of letters is taken from inside the words that follow.

parts.note: seven letters in a row that start three into the first word and finish one into the third

explanation.surface: An impassioned offer to help lay ten secrets open.
explanation.walkthrough: The run crosses two word-breaks, and the middle word of the three is swallowed whole, which is the hardest kind of hiding place to see. 'Contribution to' is doing the work 'some of' or 'part of' usually does.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody intense feels and shows more than the moment asks for, which is what calling them passionate says of them.

clue.text: Maybe "Grizzly" Idris returning is possible to live with

indicators.note: Something returning comes back along the road it went out on, so the name beside it is read from its last letter to its first.

parts.note: a grizzly is one kind of bear, and 'maybe' marks it as an example rather than a synonym
Idris Elba, the London-born actor, with his surname read backwards

explanation.surface: Somebody nicknamed Grizzly coming back, and whether anyone could stand having him around.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the actor by his first name and wants only his second, which is the step that keeps the letters hidden. Quotation marks around the nickname are the setter's way of saying the word itself is not the point.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bearable can be put up with — endured without becoming more than a person can stand.

indicators.note: To forget a thing is to lose hold of it altogether, so the letter named alongside drops out of the word.

parts.note: loath means unwilling, as in loath to admit it
the head of a word is the letter standing at its front

explanation.surface: A promise from the head that nobody much wants to remember.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is the school's in the surface and the front of a word in the wordplay. Loath is the adjective, reluctant, as against loathe, the verb for hating something.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath is a promise made binding by swearing to it, the solemn end of the same idea.

indicators.note: Something that flees runs off and is gone, so the letter named before it leaves the word it was sitting in.

parts.note: a jet of water is a spray
a = ace, the card and the flier alike

explanation.surface: A fighter pilot in a jet turning tail and running for home.
explanation.walkthrough: The three wordplay words read as one pilot, which is what stops the jet looking like water. Spry is the word kept for old people who have stayed quick on their feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry describes someone light and quick in their movements, agile said of a person rather than of a gymnast's technique.

indicators.note: Something massaged is worked over and pushed about under the hand, so the letters do not stay where they were put.

parts.note: the eight letters of those two words re-set

explanation.surface: Rubbing a balm in while still wearing one glove.
explanation.walkthrough: The instruction hides inside the action, because rubbing a balm in really is massaging it. 'On' belongs to the fodder rather than to the sentence, and counting the letters is what proves it.
explanation.definitionFit: A balm is the soothing preparation you rub into skin, and ointment is the plain word for the same tub of stuff.

indicators.note: Letters sent about are sent every which way, so the ones named will not be read in the order given.

parts.note: the nine letters of those two words re-set

explanation.surface: A diver who has worn himself out rushing around all day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tore about' is such a natural phrase that the instruction inside it goes unheard. Being overtired is past the point of ordinary tiredness, the state where sleep stops coming easily.
explanation.definitionFit: Knackered is British slang for exhausted, taken from the knacker's yard where worn-out horses ended up.

clue.text: Note about side pain that comes on suddenly

indicators.note: Something set about a thing is wrapped round it, so the letters named first close over the ones that follow.

parts.note: te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale, the one before the octave closes
a wing is a side, of a building, of an army or of a football pitch

explanation.surface: A memorandum written about a stitch in somebody's side.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to the end of the clue, five words of it, which is why nothing after 'side' looks like wordplay. 'About' here encloses rather than shuffles, and only the letter count tells you which.
explanation.definitionFit: A twinge is a brief sharp pain that arrives without warning and is gone again before you can point to it.

definitions.meaning: patting a baby on the back after a feed until the trapped air comes back up
turning this way and that, the way a lane makes its way between hedges

explanation.surface: Getting the trapped air out of something that will not sit straight.
explanation.walkthrough: To wind a baby is British for burping it, and that nursery verb is the whole of the first half. The two halves meet at 'from', which pretends the gas is coming out of the bend.
explanation.definitionFit: Winding a baby is patting the excess air out of it, while a winding road is one that bends its way along instead of running straight.

parts.note: a tot of rum is a nip, a small measure of spirits
per is the Latin for each, as in miles per hour

explanation.surface: A measure of spirits handed out to each small child.
explanation.walkthrough: The same three letters open the clue and close it, meaning a drink the first time and a child the second. Nipper is affectionate British for a young kid, still heard from grandparents.
explanation.definitionFit: A nipper is a small child in British usage, which is the sense of tot that has nothing to do with the rum ration.

indicators.note: A suspect account is not to be trusted as it stands, so the letters beside it are not in the order they should be read in.

parts.note: the seven letters of the opening word re-set

explanation.surface: People with children under suspicion of laying traps for somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' reads as the verb the police would use and is working as an adjective. The definition is three words long and begins at 'individuals', with nothing in the clue to mark the join.
explanation.definitionFit: Parents are exactly the people who have children, the relation named from the older side of it.

definitions.note: Infantry is a collective singular where the definition is plural, but British usage gives it a plural verb — the infantry are advancing — so naming them as soldiers is fair.

indicators.note: What goes after a thing follows it, so the letters named ahead of the word end up behind the rest of them.

parts.note: what is in is what is fashionable this season
a fan is somebody who loves a team, a band or a writer
to have a go at something is to try it

explanation.surface: Troops chasing off after a well-dressed sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go after' sits there as one verb meaning pursue, which is what hides the seam between the pieces. The infantry are the foot soldiers, the ones who neither ride nor drive into battle.
explanation.definitionFit: The infantry are the soldiers who fight on foot, so the plain word names them by the only job they do.

clue.text: Joint article on deer from the south

indicators.note: South is the bottom of the grid, so in a down entry something coming from the south is written upwards, last letter first.

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, the form used before a vowel
the deer is an elk, the big deer of the northern forests, with its three letters written up the grid

explanation.surface: A co-written piece about the deer they have down south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint article' reads as one thing, a paper written by two people together, and the two words belong to different halves of the clue. An elk is the largest of the deer, called a moose in North America.
explanation.definitionFit: The ankle is the hinge between leg and foot, a joint in the anatomical sense the surface never once suggests.

parts.note: to rip something is to split it along a tear
E is ecstasy, the tablet of the dance floor

explanation.surface: Dividing up a drug between people before anybody takes it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split' also means to leave in a hurry, which is the reading the surface half-offers and the wordplay ignores. E for ecstasy is one of the standing crossword drugs, alongside H and coke.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripe means grown to the point of being fit to eat, which is what is being said of a plum you can pick and consume now.

clue.text: Man that is caught during games at school

indicators.note: What happens during something happens inside it, so the letters named before it go within the ones named after.

parts.note: PE is physical education, the games lesson on a British school timetable
ie is the Latin id est, which is what that is translates
c = caught, written beside a batsman's name on a cricket scorecard

explanation.surface: A boy caught out in the middle of a school games lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: Three letters go inside a two-letter word, so the wrapper is thinner than the thing it holds. On a chessboard the things you move are called the men, which is the sense the definition wants.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess and draughts the pieces are collectively the men, so a man is one of the things standing on the board.

clue.text: Moussaka's first class food mother makes

indicators.note: The first of a word is the letter it starts on, and nothing behind that letter is wanted.

parts.note: the letter the Greek dish starts on
ilk is a class or kind, the word that survives in 'people of that ilk'

explanation.surface: Mother's moussaka being praised as first-class cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First class' reads as one phrase of praise and the two words are working separately. The definition is literal rather than a synonym, which is unusual enough to be worth noticing.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk is what a mother's body produces to feed her young, so the definition describes the thing itself rather than finding another word for it.

parts.note: re means concerning, the word standing at the head of a memo
a minder is British for a hired bodyguard, from the sense of minding somebody

explanation.surface: A note sent round about the hiring of a bodyguard.
explanation.walkthrough: Re heads a memo in real offices, which is why the first two words sit together so comfortably and why the wordplay needs them apart. Three words is all the clue has, and none of them is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Memorandum means a thing to be remembered, so a memo is by its own name a reminder.

indicators.note: To accept a thing is to take it in, so the letters named before close round what follows.

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament, the British politician elected for a constituency
the single letter, taken exactly as it stands in the clue

explanation.surface: An MP agreeing to somebody's scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' is not an article to be brushed past but the letter itself, which is the step that makes three letters out of two. A plan is a drawing of ground seen from above, which is what a map of a place is.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan in the draughtsman's sense is a view from directly overhead, the same thing a street map gives you of a town.

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver, from the Latin argentum
the reed is the thin strip of cane in the mouthpiece that vibrates to make the note

explanation.surface: A clarinet fitting finished in silver.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is past tense and so is the answer, which is what the swap has to survive. Ag comes from argentum, the Latin the periodic table kept when English moved on.
explanation.definitionFit: Two accounts that agreed matched each other — the sense of agree that is about things corresponding, not about people consenting.

clue.text: Knock back drink in front of that female dealer

indicators.note: Knocking a thing back sends it the way it came, so the word named next is written in reverse.
What stands in front of something is written before it, so the letters already made go ahead of the ones that follow.

parts.note: to sup is to drink, and those three letters are turned round
her is how you refer to that female once she has been mentioned

explanation.surface: Downing a drink standing in front of a woman who sells things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock back' is exactly what you do to a drink, which is why it goes unread as the instruction it is. A pusher sells drugs on the street, the sense of dealer the surface quietly leaves open.
explanation.definitionFit: A pusher is a street seller of drugs, and dealer is the ordinary word for the same trade.
